rewritten_text:
But I can ask you two questions, can't I?”

“You can ask,” Monks said, looking somewhat surprised. “Whether I answer is another question.”

“Which makes three,” Mr. Bumble remarked, attempting a joke.

“Is that what you expected to get from me?” the matron demanded.

“It is,” Monks replied. “The other question?”

“What are you going to do with it? Could it be used against me?”

“Never,” said Monks, “or against me either. Look here! But take one step forward and your life won't be worth a thing.”

As he spoke, he abruptly pushed the table aside. Taking hold of an iron ring set into the floorboards, he pulled open a large trapdoor directly beside Mr. Bumble's feet. That gentleman hastily retreated several paces.

“Look down,” Monks said, lowering the lantern into the opening. “You needn't be afraid of me. I could have dropped you down there quietly enough while you were sitting over it, if that had been my intention.”

Reassured by this, the matron approached the edge, and curiosity persuaded even Mr. Bumble to venture closer. Below them, muddy water, swollen by the heavy rain, swept rapidly past. Its splashing and swirling against the green, slimy piles drowned every other sound. A watermill had once stood underneath. The current churned and foamed around the few decaying posts and pieces of machinery that remained, then seemed to surge forward with fresh force once released from the obstacles that had tried in vain to check its headlong rush.

“If you threw a man's body down there, where would it be tomorrow morning?” Monks asked, swinging the lantern back and forth in the dark shaft.

“Twelve miles downriver, and cut to pieces too,” Bumble replied, recoiling at the idea.

Monks took the small packet from inside his coat, where he had hurriedly concealed it. He tied it to a lead weight lying on the floor, formerly part of a pulley, and dropped it into the current. It fell straight and true, pierced the water with a splash they could barely hear, and disappeared.

The three looked into one another's faces and seemed to breathe more easily.

“There!” Monks said, letting the trapdoor fall heavily back into place. “If the sea ever gives up its dead, as the books say it will, it'll still keep its gold and silver—and that rubbish along with them. There's nothing more to discuss. Our pleasant gathering can come to an end.”

“By all means,” said Mr. Bumble with great eagerness.

“You'll keep your mouth shut, won't you?” Monks asked, giving him a threatening look.

What kind of life could they have together while Fate still held this dreadful outcome in the balance? The wedding must be delayed, whatever the cost. On that point he was completely determined. He loved the girl passionately; when they sat together, the slightest touch of her fingers sent exquisite pleasure through every nerve. Even so, he understood his duty clearly and knew that he had no right to marry before committing the murder. Once it was done, he could stand at the altar beside Sybil Merton and place his life in her hands without any fear of wrongdoing. Once it was done, he could hold her in his arms, certain that she would never need to blush for him or lower her head in shame. But it had to be done first, and the sooner it happened, the better for them both.

Many men in his situation would have chosen the flower-strewn path of pleasure over the steep ascent of duty. Lord Arthur, however, was too conscientious to put enjoyment before principle. His love contained more than simple passion: to him, Sybil represented everything good and noble. For a moment he felt a natural revulsion at what he was required to do, but it soon disappeared. His heart assured him that this was a sacrifice, not a sin, while his reason reminded him that there was no alternative. He had to choose between living for himself and living for others. However terrible the task undoubtedly was, he knew that he must not allow selfishness to overcome love. Sooner or later, all of us face the same decision; the same question is put to everyone. Lord Arthur faced it early, before the calculating cynicism of middle age could spoil his character or the shallow, fashionable egotism of our time corrode his heart. He therefore felt no hesitation about fulfilling his duty. Fortunately, he was also no mere dreamer or idle amateur. If he had been, he would have hesitated like Hamlet and allowed indecision to undermine his purpose. Instead he was fundamentally practical. For him, life meant action rather than reflection. He possessed that rarest of qualities: common sense.

By now, the wild, confused emotions of the previous night had entirely subsided. He looked back almost with embarrassment on his frantic wanderings through the streets and his fierce emotional suffering. The very sincerity of that suffering made it seem unreal to him now. He wondered how he could have been foolish enough to rage and complain about something inevitable.

In fact, he had been entirely unaware of his influence over her. He had followed her into the shrubbery with no thought of putting it to the test. Anxious to see how she was taking Frank Churchill's engagement, he had come without any selfish motive. His only intention had been to comfort or advise her, if she gave him an opportunity. Everything else arose from the moment, from the immediate effect of what he heard upon his feelings. The delightful certainty that she was completely indifferent to Frank Churchill, that her heart was entirely free of him, had awakened the hope that he might eventually win her affection himself. But he had not expected anything now. Only when eagerness briefly overpowered judgment had he dared to hope she might say she would allow him to try to win her. The greater hopes that gradually unfolded were all the more enchanting. The affection he had asked permission to inspire, if he could, already belonged to him! Within half an hour, he had moved from profound distress to something so close to perfect happiness that no other name would serve.

Her transformation was just as complete. That single half-hour had given them both the same precious certainty of being loved and had cleared away an equal burden of ignorance, jealousy, or mistrust. His jealousy had lasted a long time, dating from Frank Churchill's arrival, or even from the expectation of it. He had fallen in love with Emma and grown jealous of Frank Churchill at about the same time; probably one feeling had made him recognize the other. Jealousy of Frank Churchill had driven him away from the country. The gathering at Box Hill had settled his decision to leave. He would spare himself another sight of attentions that Emma so readily accepted and encouraged. He had gone away to learn indifference, but he had chosen the wrong place. His brother's home contained too much domestic happiness, and presented womanhood in too appealing a form. Isabella resembled Emma too closely, differing only in conspicuous shortcomings that constantly made Emma shine in comparison. Little could have been achieved there, even with a longer stay. Nevertheless, he had firmly persisted, day after day, until that very morning's mail brought the story of Jane Fairfax. Alongside the joy he inevitably felt—and freely allowed himself to feel, since he had never thought Frank Churchill worthy of Emma—came such tender concern and intense anxiety for her that he could remain no longer. He had ridden home through the rain and walked up immediately after dinner to see how this sweetest and best of creatures, faultless despite all her faults, was bearing the discovery.
